A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Polar Express and its application to Muon. The complete 33-page v1 and 36-page v3, including figures, equations, proofs, and Appendices A–G, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-matrix experiments, GPT-2 gradient tests, 124M-parameter language-model training, and initialization and runtime experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds 774M-parameter GPT-2 results, a weight-decay comparison, and controlled experiments on head splitting and rectangular iteration.

M1.justification: The minimax/Remez construction remains. Appendix F adds first-block Gram regularization, Y = X^T X + 10^-3 I, and normalization regularization. Appendix G moves safety scaling outside coefficient generation, changing subsequent coefficients. The general normalization offset also changes from 10^-7 to 10^-2, although Algorithm 1 retains 10^-7 with additional 1.01 scaling.

E1.justification: Coverage remains FineWeb language modeling, Tiny Shakespeare gradient tests, and synthetic polar-decomposition and matrix-runtime problems. The larger model, weight decay, and head-splitting experiments change configurations and procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The main Newton–Schulz, Chen–Chow, Jordan, You, and AdamW comparisons are retained. Appendix F.1 adds evaluated head-split Muon and combined head-split/rectangular variants as internal comparators against the standard implementation. The newly cited Grishina et al. method is not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 adds GPT-Large with 774M parameters, 36 layers, width 1280, and 20 heads, alongside the retained 124M model. v3 also adds weight decay 0.1 and an Appendix F.1 design crossing four implementation variants with three learning rates. The existing one-billion-token budget, context length, batch size, and learning-rate schedule remain.

E4.justification: Appendix F.1 adds a four-condition ablation separating head splitting, restarted rectangular iteration, and their combination. v1 left head splitting for future work and reported unsuccessful preliminary rectangular-Muon experiments. Figure 7 additionally tests weight-decay robustness. Earlier lower-bound sensitivity, spectrum-aware initialization, and rectangular-runtime analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed estimates, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands for the training comparisons. The 12 runs mentioned in v3 Appendix F.1 represent four variants at three learning rates, rather than statistical replications.

E6.justification: The 124M results remain in Figure 6. New 774M Figure 1 reports validation losses of 3.340 for Polar Express, 3.398 for Jordan, and 3.400 for You. Appendix F.1 adds losses of 3.59, 3.55, 3.60, and 3.56 for its four conditions, with nearly identical runtimes. Appendix F revises the aspect-ratio-32 speedup from nearly 10x to 5x. Figure 7 adds weight-decay curves, but its caption repeats the old 124M scores inconsistently with the plot.

T1.justification: Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 and their principal proof arguments remain. Appendix D corrects the quintic and derivative equations, including replacing the erroneous 5b coefficient on x^4 with 5c. Section 2 corrects sign-interpolation identities, and Appendix B explicitly invokes nonnegativity in its bound.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a GPU-friendly polynomial polar-decomposition method, worst-case optimal polynomial compositions, rapid initial and asymptotic convergence, practical bfloat16 operation, and improved Muon training. The larger-model evidence supports these retained contributions without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds spurious negative Gram eigenvalues as a failure mechanism. Its applicability discussion shifts from unsuccessful preliminary Muon use toward preserved optimization quality but ineffective runtime savings at GPT-Small scale, suggesting larger models or more iterations as possible beneficial regimes. Section 5.2 also qualifies the weight-decay advantage with a tie against Jordan.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's pseudocode and coefficient-generation code, v3 supplies a complete bfloat16 PyTorch routine, a longer high-precision coefficient list, and access information for method and experiment repositories. It documents optimizer assignments and exclusions, weight decay, and new ablation settings. Reproducibility information expands substantially, although the normalization choices in the prose and implementation are not reconciled.

R1.justification: v3 adds Muon convergence and precursor literature, SOAP, Kimi K2, and concurrent work by Grishina, Smirnov, and Rakhuba, distinguishing the latter through global optimality and finite-precision treatment. It removes the Anil et al. citation. The central positioning relative to Chen–Chow and Zolo-pd remains.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract and edits explanatory passages throughout the introduction, related work, method discussion, and Appendix D. It removes the contents list, adds topical paragraph headings and Appendix F.1, and foregrounds implementation code. The main section sequence and Appendix A–G organization remain.

P2.justification: The lead Figure 1 changes to the 774M comparison, and a new four-panel Figure 7 presents weight-decay results. v3 adds the prominent implementation listing and redraws the general algorithm with highlighted offline and online stages. Existing convergence and appendix plots are retained, with caption, placement, and numbering adjustments.

improvement.justification: The larger-model evaluation, controlled appendix study, and runnable implementation provide a limited net gain in empirical support and usability. The appendix's finding of no runtime benefit at GPT-Small scale usefully qualifies the acceleration proposal. These gains are tempered by Figure 7's incorrect copied scores and unreconciled normalization constants; the central theory and 124M evidence were already present in v1.
